intro: ‘La vallée des cloches’ (Très lent) is the fifth and last piece of Ravel’s Miroirs, a setting of bells for piano with high chimes, repeated notes in the middle register and a deep toll that sounds after the others stop. Ravel wrote it on three staves to keep their separate rhythms clear.

sections.label: A · High chimes over tolling fourths
sections.mNote: G♯ octaves sound above a soft carillon figure.

sections.label: B · Slow chords over low octaves
sections.mNote: Très calme. The bells move in broader strokes.

sections.label: C · Melody marked largement chanté
sections.mNote: A long melody, marked largement chanté, set among the bells.

sections.label: B′ · Return of the slow chords
sections.mNote: The four-sharp key signature returns after a fermata.

sections.label: A′ · Chimes over low bell
sections.mNote: The carillon figure returns over four low, fading strokes.

cues.title: Opening bars, three bell layers
cues.text: High G♯ octaves sound in alternation. Soft sextuplets begin beneath them, and then repeated fourths enter. Each layer moves at its own speed and covers its own range of the keyboard, and the music is written on three staves that keep the layers apart.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), La vallée des cloches, bars 1–4; Kyle Fyr, Music Theory Online 26.4 (2020), paragraphs 12–14, identifies the G♯ octaves, sextuplets and fourths. https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.4/mto.20.26.4.fyr.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Maurice Delage, June 1905
cues.text: In June 1905 Ravel wrote to his pupil Maurice Delage from the Netherlands: “Yesterday, an excursion to Alkmaar: a cheese market with carillons ringing ceaselessly.” He also described windmills turning as far as he could see. The piece is dedicated to Delage.
cues.evidence: Ravel to Maurice Delage, June 1905, in Arbie Orenstein, A Ravel Reader (2003), pp. 69–70, quoted by Kyle Fyr, paragraph 3: https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.4/mto.20.26.4.fyr.html. Delage as pupil and dedicatee: https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329

cues.title: Fermata and très calme, bars 11–13
cues.text: A fermata holds the first bells. The piano continues très calme, with slow chords above low octaves. The tolling fourths from the opening carry across the join and continue while the other bells change.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 45, bars 11–13. Fyr, paragraph 16 and Example 5, traces the fourths across this join. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IMSLP02693-Ravel-Miroirs_DemetsEd.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Central melody, Largement chanté
cues.text: Largement chanté — broadly sung. A long melody begins among the repeated bell figures. Its phrases move from note to note over the sustained low bass, and it is the broadest melodic writing in the piece.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 45–47; Fyr, paragraph 15, distinguishes the central melodic carillon from the eleven shorter repeating bell figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Noon bells in Paris
cues.text: Ravel told the pianist Robert Casadesus that the piece came from the bells ringing at noon in Paris. On the piano, the chimes overlap high above the slow bass.
cues.evidence: Ravel’s remark to Casadesus is reported by Marcel Marnat, Maurice Ravel (1986), p. 184, cited by Kyle Fyr, paragraph 7. The overlapping bell figures are analysed in paragraphs 12–16. https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.4/mto.20.26.4.fyr.html

cues.title: Piano roll, 1922
cues.text: The piano roll of this piece, recorded in 1922, is sold as Ravel’s own playing. Ravel admitted that he hired a better pianist for some of the rolls, but Ronald Woodley judged that for this one the probability favours the composer. Roy Howat heard “moments of mild anarchy between the hands”.
cues.evidence: Kyle Fyr, “Mapping Ravel’s ‘La vallée des cloches’”, Music Theory Online 26.4 (2020), paragraph 30: the Duo-Art rolls marketed as the composer’s own, Ravel’s letter to Calvocoressi about recruiting a better pianist (Orenstein 2003, p. 219), Woodley (2000, p. 222), Howat (2009, p. 321) and the 1922 sessions. https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.4/mto.20.26.4.fyr.html

cues.title: End of the melody, final system
cues.text: The melody line ends, and a chord is held under a fermata, pp. The key signature of four sharps returns with the earlier très calme chords, and the low octaves continue.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 47, final system: pp, fermata, restored four-sharp signature and très calme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening carillon
cues.text: The opening carillon returns above a deep rolled chord. Ravel identified this great bell to the pianist Henriette Faure as La Savoyarde. It sounds four times, each softer than the last, and the final bar is silence, held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 48: four rolled chords marked mf, mp, p and pp, then a bar of rests. Henriette Faure, Mon maître Maurice Ravel (1978), p. 77, cited by Fyr, paragraphs 10 and 22, records Ravel’s identification of La Savoyarde.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Fermata into the très calme chords
transitions.from: A · High chimes over tolling fourths
transitions.to: B · Slow chords over low octaves
transitions.how: The sextuplets stop, and a fermata sustains the piano’s remaining resonance. The next chords, marked pp, très calme, sit over low octaves. The key signature of four sharps stays in place. The tolling fourths continue across the join into the new passage, while the metre changes to 6/4 and then to 3/4.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 45, bars 11–15; Kyle Fyr, paragraph 16 and Example 5.

transitions.title: Five flats and largement chanté
transitions.from: B · Slow chords over low octaves
transitions.how: The accented chords die away above held bass notes. Ravel changes the key signature to five flats and marks the new line largement chanté. It starts in the middle register of the keyboard, mezzo-forte, and the low notes continue beneath it. In the Demets first edition (1906) this change comes on the final system of PDF p. 45, at the start of the central section.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 45, final system: the new signature and largement chanté begin the central section.

transitions.title: A fermata before four sharps
transitions.to: B′ · Return of the slow chords
transitions.how: The melody descends over long bass notes, and the piano reaches pianissimo. A fermata separates this passage from the return of the très calme chords. The key signature changes from five flats to four sharps, and low octaves bring back the earlier accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 47, final two systems: sustained bass, fermata and return to four sharps.

transitions.title: High chimes return over a low chord
transitions.from: B′ · Return of the slow chords
transitions.how: The slow chords thin to held notes and rests. The piano resumes its high sextuplets at pianissimo, with the G♯ octave bells beside them. At bar 50 a low rolled chord sounds beneath the carillon. It is the deep bell first heard in the middle section, at bar 28.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 48; Fyr, paragraph 22, relates the rolled chord at bar 50 to its earlier appearance at bar 28.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
